additions.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CZA: Section 172(1) statement
additions.locator: s.414CZA(1) and (2); textual amendment note on S.I. 2018/860
additions.quote: Subsection (1) does not apply if the company qualifies as medium-sized in relation to that financial year
additions.why: The binding rule that turns the section 172 duty into a published account: large companies must say each year how directors had regard to the community and the environment, among other matters. Medium-sized and small companies are exempt, which is why ownership in a smaller firm has to be chosen rather than imposed. Limits: inserted in 2018; the site notes revised text may not be fully up to date.

additions.title: The Wates Corporate Governance Principles for Large Private Companies
additions.locator: Principle Six 'Stakeholder relationships and engagement', guidance on external impacts, printed page 21 (PDF page 24); Principle Three 'Director responsibilities', printed page 15; Principle Five 'Remuneration', printed page 19
additions.quote: When explaining impact on the community or environment, boards may want to refer to recognised international standards or frameworks that it follows.
additions.why: The governance code written for large private companies, the nearest code to the unlisted firms most users will be. Principle Three asks for clear lines of accountability; Principle Six asks boards to explain environmental impact; Principle Five ties pay to long-term sustainable success. Limits: voluntary, 'apply and explain'; dated December 2018; says little about sustainability by name.

additions.title: Supervisory Statement SS5/25: Enhancing banks' and insurers' approaches to managing climate-related risks
additions.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
additions.locator: Chapter 1 'Governance', paragraphs 4.2 and 4.6, printed pages 12 and 13 (PDF pages 14 and 15); paragraphs 4.40 and 4.41 on reporting and management information to the board
additions.quote: The board and executive management should assign individual responsibility for identifying, assessing and managing climate-related risks at an appropriate level of seniority
additions.why: The clearest UK regulatory statement of the criterion's middle level: a named senior individual, written into their statement of responsibilities, with regular management information to the board. Limits: sector-specific, applying to banks, building societies and insurers only; a supervisory expectation, not a rule; climate risk only; dated December 2025.

additions.title: G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance 2023
additions.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
additions.locator: Chapter VI 'Sustainability and resilience', Principle VI.C, printed page 47 (PDF page 49)
additions.quote: The corporate governance framework should ensure that boards adequately consider material sustainability risks and opportunities when fulfilling their key functions
additions.why: International comparator: the G20 and OECD standard for corporate governance, with a chapter on the board's part in sustainability added in 2023. Limits: addressed to policy makers and written chiefly for listed companies; not binding; the publisher's web page refused automated requests but the report file opened without a log-in.

additions.title: Do chief sustainability officers and CSR committees influence CSR-related outcomes? A structured literature review based on empirical-quantitative research findings
additions.publisher: Velte and Stawinoga; Journal of Management Control 31, 333-377
additions.quote: Our analysis shows that CSR committees positively influence CSR reporting and performance.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed, open access review of 48 quantitative studies on whether a board committee or a named senior officer for sustainability changes outcomes. Committees are associated with better reporting and performance; for named officers the authors find results inconclusive. This is the evidence the first-pass log could not find. Limits: a structured review, not a meta-analysis; mostly large listed companies; associations, not proof of cause.

additions.title: Executive Compensation Tied to ESG Performance: International Evidence (ECGI Finance Working Paper 825/2022)
additions.publisher: Cohen, Kadach, Ormazabal and Reichelstein; European Corporate Governance Institute
additions.locator: Abstract (working paper page; last revised 25 March 2023)
additions.quote: the adoption of ESG Pay is accompanied by improvements in key ESG outcomes, but not by improvements in financial performance
additions.why: Evidence on the criterion's top level, sustainability built into pay: across listed companies in many countries, adoption goes with better sustainability outcomes but not better financial results. Limits: working-paper page of a study later published in the Journal of Accounting Research (2023), which is behind a paywall; listed companies only; the paper reports association, and the authors themselves frame adoption as partly a response to investor pressure.

rejected.title: The Perils and Questionable Promise of ESG-Based Compensation (Bebchuk and Tallarita, ECGI Law Working Paper 671/2022)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). A critical counterweight on pay linkage based on S&P 100 companies. Not added because the abstract's key sentences exceed the 25-word limit when quoted fairly and the list already has one paper on pay; a candidate if the lead wants the opposing view cited.

rejected.title: Executive compensation with environmental and social performance (Review of Finance, 2025)
ESG-based executive compensation: state of art and future research directions (Corporate Governance, Emerald)
Board Characteristics and Corporate Social Responsibility: A Meta-Analytic Investigation (Endrikat and others, Business & Society, 2021)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403. Not read. Its finding is reported second-hand in an open review (Velte, Management Review Quarterly, 2021), which is not a substitute for the original.

rejected.title: Executive Compensation Tied to ESG Performance (SSRN and CEPR copies)
rejected.reason: SSRN returned HTTP 403; the CEPR page showed no abstract. The ECGI working-paper page was read and is cited.

rejected.title: Institute of Directors, Code of Conduct for Directors
The Wates Principles for Large Private Companies: Reporting Insights (Financial Reporting Council, 2025)
rejected.reason: Read. Examples of company reporting; nothing on who owns sustainability or how often boards see figures. Not cited.

rejected.title: OECD publication page for the G20/OECD Principles
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 on the web page; the report file on the same site opened and is the copy cited.

rejected.title: FCA Handbook, UK Listing Rules on climate disclosure; IFRS S2 on ifrs.org
rejected.reason: The IFRS page returned only introductory text without the standard; UK SRS S2, already on the list, reproduces it. The Listing Rules were not fetched.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. 'Smaller companies have no such duty' is consistent with s.414CZA(2), which also exempts medium-sized companies from the section 172 statement. The brief does not mention the Prudential Regulation Authority's SS5/25 (December 2025), which sets a named-individual expectation for banks and insurers; that is an addition, not a correction.
